01.actor: Rabbi Abba bar Zavda, Rav Huna, Rabba son of Rav Huna
01.event: Rabbi Abba bar Zavda sends a halakhic question to Rav Huna via Marei bar Mar
01.turn: Rav Huna dies before the question reaches him
01.outcome: Rav Huna's son Rabba answers in his father's name, and the ruling is traced back to Rav
01.summary: Rabbi Abba bar Zavda sent Marei bar Mar to ask Rav Huna whether the halakha follows Rabbi Elazar on bills of divorce. Meanwhile Rav Huna died, and his son Rabba answered with what his father had taught. The rest is a chain of attributions for the ruling.
01.missing: Any reaction or consequence beyond the transmission of the ruling
01.reason: Mainly a sent question and an answer (quasi-speech), but one real event intervenes (Rav Huna's death), which shifts who answers. Mainly speech with something happening is borderline under R-C7 shape 1.

02.actor: A maidservant of Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi's household
02.event: She immersed, and when she came up a bone was found between her teeth
02.turn: The bone was an interposition during immersion
02.outcome: Rabbi required her to immerse again
02.summary: A maidservant in Rabbi's household immersed, and on coming up a bone was found between her teeth. Rabbi required her to immerse a second time. The incident is cited as evidence in a legal objection.
02.missing: Any narrated action after the ruling
02.reason: An incident with a narrated happening (immersion, discovery of the bone) resolved by a ruling, close to R-C0's cow case; but it is thin and cited as legal evidence with nothing following the ruling, so it sits between borderline and not, and borderline is preferred.

03.event: Rav Yehuda, nearly blind, struggled to read and sign documents
03.turn: Ulla told him it was unnecessary, citing Rabbi Elazar and Rav Nahman who had documents read to them
03.outcome: None narrated; the Gemara adds a legal qualification
03.summary: Rav Yehuda, almost blind, took great pains to read documents himself before signing. Ulla told him he need not, since scribes read documents to Rabbi Elazar and Rav Nahman and they signed. The Gemara then limits the practice to court scribes who feared the judge.
03.missing: Whether Rav Yehuda changed his practice; any outcome
03.reason: There is a real situation (Rav Yehuda's struggle) and a response, but the response is advice in speech and no change follows; mainly speech with something happening, so borderline rather than not.

04.missing: Any event beyond a ruling and a scholarly challenge
04.reason: Ameimar's ruling and Rav Hillel's challenge citing a written list are ordinary legal discussion; seeing a list is evidence, not an event with change.

05.missing: Any action beyond finding scholars debating and disagreeing with them
05.reason: Rav Huna son of Rav Yehoshua found the Sages discussing and argued the opposite: standard rabbinic dialogue with no event or change, not a story under R-C2.

06.missing: A one-time event; only habitual practices of biblical women and the Sages' non-protest
06.reason: Reports of what Michal daughter of Saul and Jonah's wife used to do, cited as evidence of a halakhic view, with nothing following; a bare report of practice is not a story, and the figures are biblical in any case.

07.actor: Bonyam ben Nunyam, Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi
07.event: Bonyam ben Nunyam sent Rabbi a gift of fine linens
07.summary: A wealthy man, Bonyam ben Nunyam, sent Rabbi a gift of several very fine fabrics. The Gemara explains how small each could be folded and defines a term.
07.reason: A single act reported to explain a word, with no one responding and nothing following; a bare report under R-C5.

08.event: The Sages rebuke ben Azzai for preaching procreation while not marrying
08.turn: Ben Azzai explains that his soul yearns for Torah
08.outcome: He defends his choice; the world can be maintained by others
08.summary: The Sages told ben Azzai that he expounds well on procreation but does not practice it, since he never married. Ben Azzai answered that his soul yearned for Torah and the world could be sustained by others.
08.reason: Speech only, but with a personal conflict over his way of life (not merely a scholarly challenge), and an implied life choice; speech with conflict is borderline under R-C2.

09.event: A man came before Rabban Gamliel claiming he found his bride without signs of virginity
09.turn: Rabban Gamliel suggests he diverted his approach and tells a parable
09.summary: A man came before Rabban Gamliel and said he had found an open orifice. Rabban Gamliel suggested that perhaps he had diverted his approach, illustrating with a parable of a man finding a door open or locked in the dark. A second version has him suggest it was done intentionally.
09.missing: Any action after the exchange; any outcome
09.reason: Coming before a rabbi is the only event, followed by speech and a parable, with nothing changing afterwards; under R-C0's limit (Jeff 2026-10-25) this is not a story.

10.missing: The incident itself; the passage only states where the Mishnah's incident took place
10.reason: A one-line attribution of location to an incident told elsewhere, used to resolve a legal difficulty; this is the Talmud's discussion of a story, not a story.

11.event: Rava declared Rav Mari bar Rachel, son of a gentile father, fit and appointed him an official of Babylonia
11.outcome: Rav Mari became an official; the Gemara justifies the appointment
11.summary: Rava ruled that Rav Mari bar Rachel, whose father was a gentile, was of fit lineage, and appointed him as one of the officials of Babylonia. The Gemara explains why this did not violate the rule that appointees must be from among your brethren.
11.missing: Any narrated circumstance or reaction around the appointment
11.reason: A report of what Rava did, cited as precedent, followed by legal justification; but the appointment is itself an act that changes something, which per R-C0 (Ketubot 65a) keeps it borderline rather than not.

12.missing: Any one-time event with change; only recollections of study and a reconciliation of contradictory statements
12.reason: Rabbi Yohanan's recollections of studying with Rabbi Oshaya and of crowded study halls are reports of circumstance, harmonized by the Gemara; nothing happens and nothing changes.

13.actor: Ameimar; Mar Ukva; a litigant in each case
13.event: While Ameimar judged, a feather landed on his head and a man removed it; a man covered spittle before Mar Ukva
13.turn: Each asks the man his business and learns he has a case to bring
13.outcome: Each judge disqualifies himself from the man's case because of the small favor
13.summary: Ameimar was judging when a feather landed on his head; a man came and removed it. Asked what he was doing there, the man said he had a case, and Ameimar declared himself disqualified from judging it. The same happened to Mar Ukva when a man covered spittle lying before him.
13.reason: Each episode has distinct actions (the favor, the question, the recusal) and a change caused by them: the judge removes himself from the case. At least two actions and a change.

14.missing: Any event beyond teaching and a rejection
14.reason: Rabbi Zakkai recites a baraita and Rabbi Yohanan tells him to teach it outside: teaching and a rebuke, ordinary scholarly discourse, not a story.

15.event: Ravina, sitting before Rav Ashi, saw a man tying his donkey to a palm tree on Shabbat
15.turn: He shouted at the man, who ignored him, so Ravina declared him excommunicated
15.outcome: Ravina asked whether this was irreverent toward his teacher; Rav Ashi said that where God's name is desecrated, no honor is due to a teacher
15.summary: Ravina was sitting before Rav Ashi when he saw a man tie his donkey to a palm tree on Shabbat. He shouted at him, but the man paid no attention, so Ravina placed him under excommunication. Afterwards he asked Rav Ashi whether he had acted irreverently, and Rav Ashi said that where there is desecration of God's name no respect is due to a teacher.
15.reason: A one-time incident with several actions (the violation, the rebuke, being ignored, the excommunication) and a change, followed by its resolution. Rava's preceding dictum frames it.

16.actor: Rabbi Abbahu; Rabbi Ami and Rabbi Asi
16.event: Rabbi Abbahu sat and reported a ruling in Rabbi Yohanan's name
16.turn: Rabbi Ami and Rabbi Asi turned their faces away in disagreement
16.outcome: They said nothing, out of respect for his standing at Caesar's court (per Rav Pappa)
16.summary: Rabbi Abbahu sat and stated a ruling in the name of Rabbi Yohanan, and Rabbi Ami and Rabbi Asi turned their faces away in silent disagreement. Another version names Rabbi Hiyya bar Abba as the speaker. Rav Pappa explains their silence by Rabbi Abbahu's ties to Caesar's court.
16.missing: Any outcome or change beyond the silent gesture
16.reason: Mainly speech, with one non-verbal act of conflict (turning their faces); Rav Pappa's analysis is commentary. Speech with conflict and a small action is borderline.

17.turn: He asked how a woman helps a man
17.outcome: Elijah answered that she turns raw produce into bread and clothing
17.summary: Rabbi Yosei met Elijah and asked him how a wife is a helpmate. Elijah answered that she turns the wheat and flax a man brings into food and clothing, lighting up his eyes.
17.missing: Any action or change beyond the encounter and the exchange
17.reason: A setting (the encounter) plus a question and answer; per R-C2 (Shabbat 147a) a setting that only frames a Q&A is not enough for a story.

18.actor: Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi on his deathbed; the people of Bireta DeSatya; Rabbi Ahai
18.event: Dying, Rabbi prophetically described places in Babylonia
18.turn: He tells that the people of Bireta DeSatya fished on Shabbat, were excommunicated by Rabbi Ahai, and became apostates
18.outcome: He ends announcing that Adda bar Ahava is being circumcised today and Rav Yehuda was born today
18.summary: As Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi was dying, he spoke prophetically about places in Babylonia and their flawed lineage. In one, the people trapped fish on Shabbat when a ditch overflowed; Rabbi Ahai excommunicated them, and they all abandoned Judaism. He ended by announcing that Adda bar Ahava was in Abraham's lap that day and that Rav Yehuda had just been born.
18.reason: The deathbed prophecy is a narrated event and contains an embedded story with actions and causal change (Shabbat violation, excommunication, apostasy). Segment 4 is the Gemara's dictum about the righteous and is commentary, not part of it.

19.actor: Rabbi Yohanan and Rabba bar bar Hana
19.event: Rabba bar bar Hana and others would follow Rabbi Yohanan to eat Genosar fruits
19.turn: Rabbi Yohanan would eat enormous quantities
19.outcome: He would swear he had not tasted anything nourishing
19.summary: Rabba bar bar Hana recalls following Rabbi Yohanan to eat the fruits of Genosar, each person taking ten or a hundred. Rabbi Yohanan would eat them all and then swear he had not tasted anything nourishing. The Gemara corrects the wording of his oath.
19.missing: A one-time event and a change; it is a habitual report cited as evidence
19.reason: A habitual eyewitness report cited for a legal point, with actions but no change; close to R-C5's bare report, but it narrates real doings and a striking reaction, so borderline is preferred over not.

20.actor: Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi and his sons Rabbi Shimon and Rabban Gamliel
20.event: On his deathbed Rabbi calls for his younger son
20.turn: He transmits the orders of wisdom to Rabbi Shimon, then calls his older son and transmits the procedures of the Nasi's office
20.outcome: Rabban Gamliel receives the Nasi's office with the instruction to lead assertively
20.summary: Dying, Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi asked for his younger son; Rabbi Shimon came in and received the orders of wisdom. Then he asked for his older son; Rabban Gamliel came in, received the procedures of the Nasi, and was told to lead with assertiveness and cast fear on his students.
20.reason: A one-time narrated sequence of actions (summoning, entering, transmitting) with a change: succession to the leadership. Part of the larger deathbed story.
